\n<h3>L'idea</h3>\n<p>I pronomi soggetto:
The idea

Subject pronouns are the words that say who does the action: I, you, he… Just like in English, in Dutch the subject can never be left out: Ik woon in Gent, never just Woon in Gent. The verb changes very little, so the pronoun is what tells you who is speaking.

The table

Englishstressedunstressed
Iik('k)
youjijje
you (polite)uu
hehij(ie)
shezijze
ithet('t)
wewijwe
you (plural)julliejullie
theyzijze

The forms in brackets are heard in fast speech, but you don't need to use them.

Stressed or unstressed?

Many pronouns have two forms. The unstressed one (je, ze, we) is the normal one: it's what you hear most. The stressed form (jij, zij, wij) is used when you want to highlight the person, usually for contrast: Jij bent moe, ik niet (you're tired, I'm not). If in doubt, both are correct.

Jij, u and jullie

jij/je is used with friends, family and people your age. u is the polite form, for strangers, older people or at work, and works for one person or several. Careful: with u the verb is conjugated as with jij (u bent, u woont). jullie is the informal plural "you" (you all) and takes a plural verb (jullie zijn).

Zij: she or they?

zij/ze means both "she" and "they". You can tell which from the verb: zij is = she is, zij zijn = they are.

For things: hij or het

When you refer to a thing already mentioned, the pronoun depends on the noun's article (more on this in unit 3). With a noun that takes de you use hij: de tafel → hij. With a noun that takes het you use het: het boek → het. In the plural you always use ze. So to a Dutch speaker, a table is "he".

Watch out: typical mistakes

  • Leaving out the subject, especially in short answers: Ben moe → Ik ben moe.
  • Capitalising Ik in the middle of a sentence as in English "I": it's written ik, lowercase.
  • Using the hij/zij verb form with u: u is → u bent.
Nel parlato fiammingo informale al posto: In informal spoken Flemish, instead of jij/je you often hear gij/ge: "Waar woont ge?". In writing and with people you don't know, use u, which is more widespread in Belgium than in the Netherlands: many children even use it with their grandparents.
\n<h3>L'idea</h3>\n<p>In italiano il pre:
The idea

In English the present tense has hardly any endings (I work, he works). Dutch is similar: there are only three forms, so it's quite simple. The Dutch present also covers "I am working" and often the near future: Ik werk morgen = I'm working tomorrow.

How to conjugate in three steps

1. Find the stem: remove -en from the infinitive. werken → werk.
2. With ik you use the stem on its own.
3. With jij, u, hij, zij (she), het you add -t. In the plural (wij, jullie, zij) you use the whole infinitive.

werken (to work)wonen (to live)
ikwerkwoon
jij / uwerktwoont
hij / zij / hetwerktwoont
wij / jullie / zijwerkenwonen

The spelling rules

The sound never changes: only the spelling does, to keep the same sound when the word gets shorter.

  • Long vowel: in wo-nen the o is long but written single, because the syllable ends in a vowel. When you remove -en the syllable closes, and to keep the long sound you have to double the vowel: woon. In the same way maken → maak, lopen → loop.
  • Double consonant: zitten → zit, liggen → lig. Dutch never writes two identical consonants at the end of a word.
  • v → f and z → s at the end of a word: leven → leef, lezen → lees.
  • If the stem already ends in -t you don't add another t: zitten → hij zit. If it ends in -d you still add the t, even though you can't hear it: vinden → hij vindt.

Questions with jij/je

In questions the verb goes first (unit 7). When jij/je follows the verb, the -t drops: Jij werkt but Werk je? This applies only to jij/je: Werkt hij? Werkt u? keep the t.

  • Translating "I am working" word for word: ik werk is enough.

\n<h3>L'idea</h3>\n<p>L'italiano ha molt:
The idea

English has just one definite article, "the". Dutch has two: de and het. de is used for masculine and feminine nouns, het for neuter nouns. In the Netherlands masculine and feminine are now one single group; in Belgium many speakers still tell them apart (de tafel → hij, de deur → ze). About two nouns in three take de.

There's only one indefinite article: een (a, an), for all nouns. In the indefinite plural there's no article: boeken = books, some books.

Useful rules

  • The plural always takes de: het boek → de boeken.
  • Diminutives in -je are always het: het meisje, het huisje.
  • Languages are het: het Nederlands, het Engels.
  • An infinitive used as a noun is het: het eten (eating, food).
  • Words beginning with ge-, be-, ver- are often het, unless they end in -ing, -te or -er: het gesprek, het verhaal (but de vergadering).
  • Many words in -ment are het: het appartement, het moment.
  • People and professions are almost always de: de man, de vrouw, de dokter. Exceptions to remember: het kind and het meisje.

Why it matters

There's no rule that covers every noun, so the practical advice is simple: learn every noun together with its article, as you find it in the word list. The article also decides other things you'll see later: the pronoun (hij or het, unit 1), and the form of adjectives and demonstratives.

de-wordhet-word
definitede stadhet huis
indefiniteeen stadeen huis
pluralde stedende huizen

Watch out: typical mistakes

  • Thinking that "the girl" must be feminine: it's het meisje, because it's a diminutive.
  • Putting an article before languages: "I speak Dutch" is Ik spreek Nederlands, without an article, just like in English.
  • Using het in the plural: it's always de.

\n<h3>L'idea</h3>\n<p>I pronomi oggetto:
The idea

Object pronouns are words like me, him, her, us, them: they show who receives the action. As in English, they go after the verb: Ik zie hem (I see him). And as in English, the same form is used after prepositions: met mij (with me), voor jou (for you), van hem (from him).

The table

subjectobjectEnglish
ikmij / meme
jijjou / jeyou
uuyou (polite)
hijhemhim
zij (she)haarher
hethetit
wijonsus
julliejullieyou (plural)
zij (they)hen / hun / zethem

As with subjects, me and je are the unstressed, normal forms. mij and jou are for emphasis or after prepositions: Ik wacht op jou, niet op hem.

"Them": hen, hun or ze?

In formal writing hen is used as a direct object and after prepositions (Ik zie hen, met hen), hun as an indirect object, meaning "to them" (Ik geef hun een cadeau). In speech almost everyone just says ze: Ik zie ze. When speaking, use ze.

Things: hem, het, ze

Here the article matters again. A thing with de becomes hem, where English would say "it": De sleutel? Ik zoek hem (the key? I'm looking for it). A thing with het becomes het. Things in the plural become ze.

Watch out: typical mistakes

  • Putting the pronoun before the verb: Ik hem zie → Ik zie hem.
  • Using the subject form after a preposition: met ik → met mij.
  • Using het for every thing as with English "it": the key is de sleutel, so hem.
In Fiandra \"<b>ik zie u graag</b>\" sig: In Flanders "ik zie u graag" means "I love you" and is said in families and between partners: here u isn't formal: it's the object form of gij/ge (gij → u, like jij → je). In the Netherlands you'd say "ik hou van je".
\n<h3>Da 0 a 20</h3>\n<p>0 nul · 1 een ·:
From 0 to 20

0 nul · 1 een · 2 twee · 3 drie · 4 vier · 5 vijf · 6 zes · 7 zeven · 8 acht · 9 negen · 10 tien · 11 elf · 12 twaalf

From 13 to 19 you join the unit to tien, with a few small changes: 13 dertien (not drietien), 14 veertien (not viertien), 15 vijftien, 16 zestien, 17 zeventien, 18 achttien, 19 negentien. 20 is twintig.

The tens

20 twintig · 30 dertig · 40 veertig · 50 vijftig · 60 zestig · 70 zeventig · 80 tachtig · 90 negentig. The forms in bold are the irregular ones to memorise.

From 21 to 99: units first

Here's the big difference from English: you say the unit first, then en (and), then the ten, all in one word. It's like saying "one-and-twenty" instead of "twenty-one".

numberDutchliterally
21eenentwintigone and twenty
35vijfendertigfive and thirty
47zevenenveertigseven and forty
88achtentachtigeight and eighty

When two e's meet you add a diaeresis: 22 tweeëntwintig, 23 drieëntwintig.

Hundreds, thousands and years

100 is honderd (without "een" in front), 200 tweehonderd, 1000 duizend. 2026 = tweeduizend zesentwintig. Years before 2000 are said in hundreds: 1990 = negentienhonderdnegentig (nineteen-hundred-ninety).

Prices, decimals and measures

  • Dutch uses a decimal comma, read as komma: 2,5 = twee komma vijf.
  • In prices the comma isn't read: €3,50 = drie euro vijftig.
  • Units of measurement stay singular: twee kilo, honderd gram, drie liter.

Ordinals (first, second…)

Up to 19 you add -de: tweede, vierde, vijfde. Three exceptions: eerste (first), derde (third), achtste (eighth). From 20 up you add -ste: twintigste, honderdste.

Watch out: typical mistakes

  • Reversing the order: 21 is not twintigeen but eenentwintig.
  • Using "have" for age: Ik heb dertig jaar → Ik ben dertig jaar, as in English "I am thirty".
  • Putting measures in the plural: twee kilos → twee kilo.
I belgi francofoni dicono \"septante\" e: French-speaking Belgians say "septante" and "nonante", but in Dutch it's always zeventig and negentig. When you pay they'll ask "Met Bancontact?", and you'll hear "alstublieft" as a reply to "dank u" too: in Belgium it also means "you're welcome".
\n<h3>L'idea</h3>\n<p>In italiano il plu:
The idea

As in English, Dutch forms the plural by adding an ending. There are two main endings: -en and -s. Remember that in the plural the article is always de.

Which ending?

  • -en is the general rule: boek → boeken, fiets → fietsen.
  • -s for words ending in -el, -em, -en, -er, -je (weak final syllable): tafel → tafels, meisje → meisjes, kamer → kamers.
  • -'s (with an apostrophe) for words ending in a, i, o, u, y: auto → auto's, menu → menu's. The apostrophe keeps the vowel long.

Spelling with -en

It's the same logic as for verbs (unit 2): the sound stays the same, the spelling changes.

  • A long vowel written double becomes single, because the syllable opens: boom → bo-men, jaar → ja-ren.
  • Short vowel: you double the consonant to keep it short: man → man-nen, bus → bus-sen.
  • f → v and s → z between two vowels: brief → brieven, huis → huizen.

Irregular ones to memorise

singularplural
het kindde kinderen
het eide eieren
de stadde steden
het schipde schepen

Watch out: typical mistakes

  • Keeping the double vowel: boomen → bomen.
  • Forgetting the apostrophe: autos → auto's.
  • Using het in the plural: het kinderen → de kinderen.
Le patatine fritte in Belgio sono <b>fri: Fries in Belgium are frieten (de friet, de frieten) and you buy them at a frituur or "frietkot". In the Netherlands you'd say "patat". In speech, especially in the Netherlands, the final -n of the plural is often not pronounced: "boeke".
\n<h3>Domande sì/no: il verbo va all'ini:
Yes/no questions: the verb goes first

English makes questions with "do" or by moving the auxiliary ("Do you speak Dutch?", "Is he coming?"). Dutch has no "do": you simply swap the order, putting the verb in first position, before the subject.

statementquestion
Hij spreekt Frans.Spreekt hij Frans?
Jij woont in Gent.Woon je in Gent?
U komt morgen.Komt u morgen?

Remember the rule from unit 2: before je/jij the -t of the verb drops.

Questions with a question word

The order is: question word + verb + subject + rest.

DutchEnglishexample
wiewhoWie is dat?
watwhatWat doe je?
waarwhereWaar woon je?
wanneerwhenWanneer kom je?
waaromwhyWaarom leer je Nederlands?
hoehowHoe heet je?
hoeveelhow much / how manyHoeveel kost dat?

Welke or welk?

"Which" is welke, except before a singular het-word, where it's welk: welk huis? but welke fiets? and welke huizen?

Where from: waar … vandaan

"Where are you from?" is Waar kom je vandaan? The word waar goes at the start and vandaan at the end of the sentence.

Hoe heet je?

To ask someone's name you use hoe (how), not wat: Hoe heet je? Literally "how are you called?"

Watch out: typical mistakes

  • Making a question only with intonation: Je woont in Gent? → Woon je in Gent?
  • Putting the subject before the verb after the question word: Waar je woont? → Waar woon je?
  • Using wat for a name, as in "what's your name": Wat heet je? → Hoe heet je?
Senti spesso \"<b>Hoe gaat het met u?</b: You often hear "Hoe gaat het met u?" even in informal settings. A typical answer is "Goed, merci!": Flemish people often say merci for thank you, alongside "dank u".
\n<h3>L'idea</h3>\n<p>I possessivi dicon:
The idea

Possessives say whose something is. They work much like in English: no article in front ("my book" is mijn boek), and the possessive depends on the owner: zijn moeder is his mother, haar moeder is her mother.

The table

personpossessiveexample
ikmijnmijn naam
jijjouw / jejouw fiets
uuwuw jas
hijzijnzijn moeder
zij (she)haarhaar vader
wijons / onzeons huis, onze stad
julliejullie / jejullie kinderen
zij (they)hunhun boeken

Ons or onze?

It's the only possessive that changes. ons before a singular het-word (ons huis), onze in all other cases: de-words (onze stad) and plurals (onze kinderen).

Jouw or je?

As with pronouns, je is the unstressed and more common form: Is dat je fiets?. jouw is for emphasis: Is dat jouw fiets of mijn fiets?

"It's mine": van mij

When the possessive stands alone, after the verb, you use van + object pronoun: Van wie is dat? — Het is van mij (whose is that? — it's mine). With names you use van, not 's: de fiets van Tom (Tom's bike).

Watch out: typical mistakes

  • Adding an article: de mijn auto → mijn auto.
  • Saying "Tom's fiets" in everyday speech: the usual form is de fiets van Tom.
  • Using ons with a de-word: ons stad → onze stad.
Nel parlato fiammingo, insieme a gij/ge,: In spoken Flemish, together with gij/ge, uw is used between friends too: "Is dat uw fiets?" can be completely informal.
\n<h3>L'idea</h3>\n<p>I verbi modali son:
The idea

Modal verbs are the ones like can, must, want to: they're used together with another verb in the infinitive. The most important rule is about position: the conjugated modal is in second place and the infinitive goes to the end of the sentence. The two parts form a kind of "frame".

Ik wil morgen met de trein naar Gent gaan. (I want to go to Ghent by train tomorrow.)

What each one means

  • kunnen: to be able to, can. Ik kan zwemmen (I can swim). Kun je morgen komen? (can you come tomorrow?)
  • mogen: to be allowed, may. Mag ik hier parkeren? (may I park here?). niet mogen = it's not allowed: Je mag hier niet roken.
  • moeten: must, to have to. Ik moet werken. Careful: "don't have to" in the sense of "it's not necessary" uses another verb, hoeven, which you'll see later.
  • willen: to want. Ik wil koffie. To ask politely, add graag: Ik wil graag koffie (I'd like a coffee).
  • zullen: future, promise or offer. Ik zal je helpen (I'll help you). Zal ik je helpen? (shall I help you?)

Conjugation

Modals are irregular in the singular: with ik, hij and zij they have no -t.

kunnenmoetenwillenmogenzullen
ikkanmoetwilmagzal
jij / ukunt / kanmoetwilt / wilmagzult / zal
hij / zijkanmoetwilmagzal
wij / jullie / zijkunnenmoetenwillenmogenzullen

Without the infinitive

With movement the infinitive is often left out, because it's obvious: Ik moet naar huis (I have to go home), Ik wil naar Brugge.

Watch out: typical mistakes

  • Putting the infinitive right after the modal, as in English: Ik wil gaan morgen naar Gent → Ik wil morgen naar Gent gaan.
  • Adding -t with hij: hij kant → hij kan.
  • Adding te after a modal, like English "to": Ik wil te gaan → Ik wil gaan.
Per il futuro nel parlato si usa molto <: For the future, speech often uses gaan + infinitive: "Ik ga dat morgen doen" (I'm going to do it tomorrow). "Ge moogt" (= je mag, you may) is typically Flemish.
\n<h3>L'idea: il verbo in seconda posizi:
The idea: the verb in second position

English word order is fairly fixed around subject-verb. Dutch has a different fixed rule for the main clause: the conjugated verb is always in second place. First place can be the subject, but also another part of the sentence.

1st place2nd (verb)rest
Ikwerkvandaag thuis.
Vandaagwerkik thuis.
Thuiswerkik vandaag.

Inversion

If you put something that isn't the subject in first place (a time expression, a place, an object), the subject moves after the verb. This is called inversion: Morgen ga ik naar Brugge, never Morgen ik ga. It's the most common mistake for English speakers, because English says "Tomorrow I go".

Time – manner – place

When a sentence contains several details, the usual order is: when, then how, then where. English often does the opposite.

Ik ga morgen met de trein naar Gent. (I'm going to Ghent by train tomorrow.)

The frame with two verbs

With a modal verb (unit 9) the conjugated verb stays in second place and the infinitive goes to the end: Vanavond willen we in Gent eten.

Conjunctions

en (and), maar (but), of (or) and want (because, since) don't count as a position: after them the order stays normal. Ik blijf thuis, want ik ben moe.

dus (so) is more flexible: it can take first place (Ik ben moe, dus blijf ik thuis) or behave like want (dus ik blijf thuis). Both are correct.

Watch out: typical mistakes

  • Forgetting inversion: Vandaag ik werk → Vandaag werk ik.
  • Putting place before time, as in English: Ik ga naar Gent morgen → Ik ga morgen naar Gent.
  • Inverting after want: want ben ik moe → want ik ben moe.
Le regole sono identiche in tutto il ter: The rules are the same everywhere; the vocabulary changes. In Flanders you say een broodje smos (a sandwich with salad), de gsm (the mobile phone) and 's voormiddags (in the morning).
di pomeriggio (in Belgio spesso: verso m: in the afternoon (in Belgium often: around midday)
